question: On the Mac-apollo cable, where does rsync still beat xs, does PR #34's compression pick well on fast hosts, and which settings should be xs's defaults?

nodes.title: Compression at 10 GbE
nodes.question: At full link speed with fast CPUs, does xs-rs -z at its automatic level (PR #34) keep up with the best fixed level, and with no compression?
nodes.hypothesis: On 10 GbE with fast CPUs, xs-rs -z at its automatic level (PR #34) is within 5% of the fastest fixed level and of no compression.
nodes.decision: CZ1: a fixed zstd level beat PR #34's automatic choice at 10 GbE: confirm it, and the policy needs another look (large-text mac→apollo xs-rs-z1 2.20× [0.27, 18.04]; large-text mac→apollo xs-rs-z3 1.41× [0.11, 18.04]; large-text apollo→mac xs-rs-z3 1.17× [0.86, 1.59]; real-congress mac→apollo xs-rs-z3 1.15× [0.29, 4.52]; 2 more)

nodes.title: Confirm the faster fixed level
nodes.question: Does the fixed level that beat the automatic one do it again on eight fresh blocks?
nodes.hypothesis: Confirms the fastest arm of CZ1 with 8 fresh blocks, if it had one.

nodes.title: Take the delta loss apart
nodes.question: On delta updates of large files, where rsync won RW1, is it xs's delta path or its copy that loses, and does --whole-file win at 10 GbE?
nodes.hypothesis: rsync is at least 5% faster than xs in some delta cell, and xs with --whole-file shows whether xs's delta path or its copy is the cause.
nodes.decision: RW7: xs with --whole-file beat rsync's delta at 10 GbE: on a fast link xs should skip the delta; confirm (large-solo mac→apollo xs-cpp-W 2.66× [0.00, 11261.27]; hs-16x256m mac→apollo xs-rs-W 2.38× [0.00, 2255.51]; large-solo mac→apollo xs-cpp-W 2.30× [0.00, 657178.09]; large-text mac→apollo xs-cpp-W 1.83× [0.00, 1734.90]; 17 more)

nodes.title: Confirm --whole-file on fast links
nodes.question: Does xs with --whole-file beat rsync's delta again on eight fresh blocks?
nodes.hypothesis: xs-rs-W is more than 5% faster than rsync on large-text (from RW7-delta-breakdown-apollo, confirmed with fresh blocks).

nodes.title: Deltas over a 20 ms round trip
nodes.question: Over a 20 ms round trip, does rsync's delta beat xs's?
nodes.hypothesis: Over a 20 ms round trip, rsync is at least 5% faster than xs in some delta cell.
nodes.decision: RW8a: latency widens rsync's delta lead: xs's signature exchange costs round trips (large-text apollo→mac xs-rs 0.91× [0.45, 1.82]; hs-16x256m apollo→mac xs-rs 0.86× [0.82, 0.90]; hs-16x256m apollo→mac xs-rs 0.84× [0.67, 1.06]; hs-16x256m apollo→mac xs-cpp 0.84× [0.63, 1.11]; 13 more)

nodes.title: Deltas on a slow, distant path
nodes.question: On a 20 ms, 100 Mb/s path, where sending only the changes matters most, does rsync's delta beat xs's?
nodes.hypothesis: Over a 20 ms, 100 Mb/s path, rsync is at least 5% faster than xs in some delta cell.
nodes.decision: RW8b: on a slow path rsync's delta beats xs: xs must send less when bytes are the limit; a code case (large-text apollo→mac xs-rs 0.85× [0.77, 0.94]; large-text apollo→mac xs-rs 0.80× [0.71, 0.90]; large-text apollo→mac xs-cpp 0.52× [0.51, 0.52]; large-text mac→apollo xs-cpp 0.47× [0.01, 27.43]; 1 more)

nodes.title: Finish the many-file no-ops
nodes.question: With three more blocks, does xs keep its lead at no-ops of many files?
nodes.hypothesis: rsync is at least 5% faster to durable than xs-c++ or xs-rs in some cell. No-ops of many files, where NT1021 saw rsync pull real-psample in 75.7 s against xs-cpp 151.6 s; -j1 arms for a per-core comparison.

nodes.title: Hard links, checked again
nodes.question: With hard links kept (-H) on laikav2, is xs-c++ as fast as rsync, over six blocks?
nodes.hypothesis: rsync is at least 5% faster to durable than xs-c++ or xs-rs in some cell. Hard links kept with -H, on laikav2 (1,234 linked files in its Rust target folder). xs-rs has no -H, so it sits out.

nodes.title: PR #34 against its base
nodes.question: Is xs-rs at PR #34 at least as fast as the xs-rs it changes, in every cell at 10 GbE?
nodes.hypothesis: xs-rs at PR #34 is within 5% of its base or faster in every cell at 10 GbE.
nodes.decision: PR1: PR #34 is slower than its base in some cell: confirm on fresh blocks before merging (hs-16x256m apollo→mac xs-rs 0.82× [0.29, 2.34]; local-laikav2 apollo→mac xs-rs 0.81× [0.30, 2.18])

nodes.title: Confirm the PR #34 regression
nodes.question: On eight fresh blocks, is PR #34 really slower than its base where PR1 said so?
nodes.hypothesis: xs-rs at PR #34 is within 5% of its base or faster in every cell at 10 GbE.

nodes.title: Compression at 1 Gb/s
nodes.question: Held to 1 Gb/s, does the automatic level keep up with the best fixed level?
nodes.hypothesis: Held to 1 Gb/s, xs-rs -z at its automatic level is within 5% of the fastest fixed level.
nodes.decision: CZ2: at 1 Gb/s a fixed level beat the automatic one: the rate rule's thresholds need moving (large-text apollo→mac xs-rs-z3 1.44× [1.44, 1.44]; large-text mac→apollo xs-rs-z3 1.15× [0.00, 429.31])

nodes.title: Compression at 100 Mb/s
nodes.question: Held to 100 Mb/s, does the automatic level keep up with the best of levels 1, 3 and 6, and does compression beat none?
nodes.hypothesis: Held to 100 Mb/s, xs-rs -z at its automatic level is within 5% of the fastest fixed level, and compression beats none.
nodes.decision: CZ3: at 100 Mb/s a fixed level beat the automatic one: the policy should climb sooner when bytes are the limit (real-congress mac→apollo xs-rs-z3 1.20× [1.00, 1.43]; real-congress mac→apollo xs-rs-z1 1.19× [0.58, 2.47])

nodes.title: Compression on two cores
nodes.question: With apollo held to 2 cores on the fast link, does the automatic level stay within 5% of the best?
nodes.hypothesis: With apollo held to 2 cores, xs-rs -z at its automatic level is within 5% of the fastest fixed level.
nodes.decision: CZ4: with 2 cores a fixed level beat the automatic one: the CPU veto misjudges this machine (large-text mac→apollo xs-rs-z1 1.44× [0.00, 772.06])

nodes.title: Small files onto the Mac
nodes.question: Writing small files onto the Mac's APFS, does --no-atomic or more workers make xs faster, and is xs at least as fast as rsync?
nodes.hypothesis: Pulling small files onto the Mac, xs --no-atomic is at least 5% faster than xs's default, and xs is at least as fast as rsync.
nodes.decision: SM1: skipping the rename or more workers writes small files onto APFS faster: confirm (scale-count-1000000 apollo→mac xs-cpp-noatomic 1.76× [1.67, 1.86]; real-congress apollo→mac xs-cpp-noatomic 1.42× [1.38, 1.45]; real-congress apollo→mac xs-cpp-j8 1.18× [0.89, 1.58]; real-congress apollo→mac xs-cpp-noatomic 1.08× [0.71, 1.63])

nodes.title: Confirm the faster APFS setting
nodes.question: Does the setting that wrote small files onto the Mac faster do it again on eight fresh blocks?
nodes.hypothesis: xs-cpp-noatomic is more than 5% faster than xs-cpp on real-congress, scale-count-1000000 (from SM1-small-onto-mac-apollo, confirmed with fresh blocks).

nodes.title: Pull psample onto the Mac
nodes.question: Pulling the 21 GB psample tree onto the Mac, does --no-atomic, -O or 8 workers beat xs's default, and is xs at least as fast as rsync?
nodes.hypothesis: Pulling psample onto the Mac, some xs setting is at least 5% faster than xs's default, and xs is at least as fast as rsync.

nodes.title: Confirm the psample pull setting
nodes.question: Does the setting that recovered the psample pull hold up on fresh blocks?
nodes.hypothesis: Confirms the fastest arm of PS1 with 6 fresh blocks, if it had one.

nodes.title: Eager writeback on Linux
nodes.question: On a Linux receiver, does eager writeback get xs's copies onto disk sooner?
nodes.hypothesis: With eager writeback on apollo, xs reaches durable at least 5% sooner than with default writeback.

nodes.title: Confirm eager writeback
nodes.question: Does eager writeback shorten xs's time to durable again on eight fresh blocks?
nodes.hypothesis: Confirms the fastest arm of WB1 with 8 fresh blocks, if it had one.

nodes.title: The ssh ceiling
nodes.question: On large files, how far is xs from a bare tar pipe on 1 and 8 streams: how much of the ceiling is the one ssh connection?
nodes.hypothesis: A bare pipe on 8 streams is at least 5% faster than xs on large files over the cable.

nodes.title: 20 ms of latency
nodes.question: Over a 20 ms round trip, does rsync beat xs at fresh copies, no-ops or 1% updates?
nodes.hypothesis: Over a 20 ms round trip, rsync is at least 5% faster than xs in some cell.

nodes.title: 80 ms of latency
nodes.question: Over an 80 ms round trip, a long internet path, does rsync beat xs anywhere?
nodes.hypothesis: Over a 80 ms round trip, rsync is at least 5% faster than xs in some cell.

nodes.title: csearchv3 with PR #34
nodes.question: On the user's csearchv3 tree, is xs-rs at PR #34 faster than its base and than rsync, fresh, at a no-op and at a 10% update?
nodes.hypothesis: On csearchv3, xs-rs at PR #34 is at least as fast as its base and faster than rsync at fresh, no-op and a 10% update.

nodes.title: Everyday incremental backups
nodes.question: On congress with 0.1%, 1% and 10% of files edited, the everyday incremental backup, does rsync beat xs?
nodes.hypothesis: rsync is at least 5% faster than xs at some incremental sync of a real tree.

nodes.title: How many xs-rs workers
nodes.question: PR #34 gives xs-rs 8 sender workers by default: is 8 the best at 10 GbE, against 1, 2, 4 and 16?
nodes.hypothesis: Some worker count is at least 5% faster than xs-rs's default of 8 in some cell.

nodes.title: Large files with PR #34
nodes.question: On 4 GiB of incompressible data in 1 to 64 files, is PR #34 at least as fast as the xs-rs it changes?
nodes.hypothesis: On 4 GiB of incompressible data, xs-rs at PR #34 is at least as fast as its base in every file count.

nodes.title: An internet-like path
nodes.question: Over a 40 ms, 1 Gb/s path, like a home link to a remote host, does xs-rs -z at its automatic level beat rsync -az and xs-c++ -z?
nodes.hypothesis: Over a 40 ms, 1 Gb/s path, xs-rs -z at its automatic level is at least as fast as rsync -az and xs-c++ -z.

nodes.title: A 1% update of psample
nodes.question: On the 21 GB psample tree with 1% of files edited and hard links kept, does rsync -aH beat xs -aH?
nodes.hypothesis: rsync -aH is at least 5% faster than xs -aH at a 1% update of psample.

nodes.title: Checksum no-ops on large files
nodes.question: With -c on trees of large files (psample, laikav2), where hashing dominates, does rsync beat xs?
nodes.hypothesis: rsync -c is at least 5% faster than xs -c at a no-op on a tree of large files.

nodes.title: Deletes at scale
nodes.question: When 10% of a large tree's files are gone, is xs --delete as fast as rsync --delete?
nodes.hypothesis: rsync --delete is at least 5% faster than xs --delete when 10% of a large tree's files are gone.

nodes.title: How many xs-c++ workers
nodes.question: Is 4 the best worker count for xs-c++ at 10 GbE, against 1, 2, 8 and 16?
nodes.hypothesis: Some worker count is at least 5% faster than xs-c++'s default of 4 in some cell.

nodes.title: A weak receiver
nodes.question: With the receiver held to 2 cores, like a small NAS, which tool and worker count is fastest?
nodes.hypothesis: With the receiver held to 2 cores, rsync is at least 5% faster than xs in some cell, or fewer xs workers are faster than the default.

nodes.title: Congress sentinel
nodes.question: Until Sunday: do rsync, xs-c++ and xs-rs keep their congress ranking, and what is the noise floor at each hour?
nodes.hypothesis: rsync, xs-c++ and xs-rs keep their congress ranking through the weekend.
